name: UVB-76
title: A Buzz on 4625 kHz, and the Voice That Interrupts It
claims: UVB-76 nicknamed "the Buzzer" broadcasts on 4625 kHz in upper sideband | 1
Buzz repeats at roughly 25 tones per minute, 24 hours a day | 1
Buzz lasts about 1.2 seconds, pauses 1–1.3 seconds, repeats 21–34 times per minute | 1
Russian nickname Zhuzhzhalka | 1
Purpose never confirmed by government or broadcast officials | 1
Earliest preserved recording is from 1982 | 1
Origin and operators unidentified at the time of early detection | 1
First voice transmission was in 1997 | 1
Location and callsign unknown until first known voice broadcast of 1997 | 1
Station identified itself as UZB-76 from 1997 to 2010 | 1
UVB-76 is a mistranscription and was never used by the station | 1
Main callsign changed regularly afterwards; side callsigns used less often and discarded when main callsign changes | 1
Voice messages always in Russian by a live voice, three formats: Monolith, Uzor, Komanda | 1
Monolith: callsigns read twice, four symbols each, five-digit ID groups, blocks of code word plus eight digits; most common has one of each | 1
Uzor: callsigns read twice, blocks of code word plus four digits; rarely sent after 2023 | 1
Komanda: rarest, callsign twice, phrase "command announced", then a number; not heard for years | 1
Background conversations and noises suggest tone made by a device near a live open microphone | 1
Pitch fluctuation suggests tonewheel like a Hammond organ; microphone may have been turned on accidentally | 1
3 November 2001 a conversation in Russian was heard | 1
Before June 2010 a continuous alternating tone replaced the buzz one minute before the hour; stopped in June 2010 | 1
September 2010 portions of buzzer replaced with Swan Lake excerpts | 1
Buzz tones lasted about 0.8 seconds until November 2010 | 1
Former transmitter near Povarovo, about 10 km northwest of Moscow near the village of Lozhki | 1
In September 2010 transmitter moved near Saint Petersburg (Kerro Massiv), possibly due to military reorganization | 1
Since 9 August 2015 not transmitting from Kerro Massiv; now appears to broadcast from the 69th Communication Hub in Naro-Fominsk | 1
In 2011 urban explorers claimed to find an abandoned military base at Povarovo with a radio log record confirming a 4625 kHz transmitter | 1

Underground bunker with small entrance structure, dark corridors and rooms, humming generators, flooded corridors frozen to ice, map of military town, instructions for staff, soot, ripped-out fittings | 2
The buzzer moved in summer 2010 | 2
Not related to Dead Hand system; interrupted many times with no retaliation | 1
BBC article theory: connected to Perimeter system, dead hand signal; unlikely because signal frequently breaks down or is switched off for maintenance | 1
Numbers-station theory (FSB/KGB) considered unlikely: unpredictable message times, static frequency, low transmitter power unsuitable for long-range | 1
Russian Journal of Earth Sciences speculation about ionosphere observatory at 4625 kHz | 1
Former Lithuanian communications minister wrote voice messages confirm receiving operators are alert; another explanation is military commissariats listening | 1
Buzz functions as channel marker keeping frequency occupied; usable for tuning, squelch, and signal-loss alarm | 1
Best-supported theory: military command network for the Leningrad Military District | 1
Similar stations nicknamed "The Pip" and "The Squeaky Wheel" | 1
15 May 2020 French-speaking persons heard | 1
January 2022 spectrogram-encoded images broadcast on the frequency | 1
Songs including "Gangnam Style" reported; Vice attributed to pirates and questioned their nationality in relation to Russo-Ukrainian crisis and war | 1
4 May 2024 at 21:38 MSK Russian-speaking pirate contacted the station while buzzer inactive or on standby, asked improvised questions, briefly conversed with operator | 1
Day before, interference prompted operator to combine three transmitters, with MS-5 burst, CIS-12 and tones, for around half an hour until pirate abandoned attempts and buzzer reactivated | 1
11 November 2025 twenty-four messages comprising thirty different words, most verbose in its history | 1
30 December 2025 hijacker broadcast Swan Lake theme and a Bremen Town Musicians song on the frequency and its Telegram channel | 1
31 December 2025 hijacked again to play Russian rap, Western pop and 1990s songs for over three hours; hijackers unknown | 1
